summary: Lists the essential requirements for real-time text over IP, such as typed conversation like live chat, and defines a framework to build it with SIP and RTP. It also covers interworking with text telephony on the phone network and other networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Real-time text sends each letter as you type, like a conversation by keyboard. This paper explains how to do that over internet calls.

questions: what is real-time text over ip
how does toip work with sip
can toip work with old text phones
subtitle: Keyboard conversation as immediate as voice, using internet protocols.

tldr.problem: Real-time text conversation, character-by-character as you type, can offer an equivalent to voice for deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired users, but needs a standard way to send it over IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a framework using SIP to set up text sessions and RTP to carry the text in real time, with requirements for low delay, interworking with legacy phone text services, and transcoding to speech.
tldr.outcome: The framework enables text conversation that runs alongside or instead of voice, connects to traditional text phones and cellular networks, and supports relay services for accessibility.

today: RFC 5194 is informational and describes a framework that has influenced implementations of real-time text in SIP systems. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Real-Time Text for Internet Calls
sections.content:
Real-time text, also called interactive text or text conversation, sends each character as the user types it, not buffered by lines or messages. For decades, deaf, hard-of-hearing and speech-impaired people have used this on text phones; this RFC extends it to internet-based calls.

The RFC defines ToIP (Text-over-IP), a conversational text service equivalent to voice telephony, built on SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) for setup and RTP (Real-Time Transport Protocol) for delivery. It is compatible with existing VoIP, video, and multimedia sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time text is like talking by keyboard in real time, one letter at a time. This paper shows how to do it on the internet like a video call.

sections.title: What Real-Time Text Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists 45 requirements covering five areas. Session control requires the ability to start, switch, or add text at any time (even mid-call), and to combine text with voice and video. Transport demands character transmission within 300ms of entry, at up to 30 characters per second, and support for all international character sets.

Transcoding services (speech-to-text and text-to-speech) must be negotiable in real time. User presentation requires clear identification of speakers, accessible alerts for deaf-blind users, and the option to save conversations. Interworking demands compatibility with text phones on the PSTN, mobile networks, instant messaging, and relay services.
sections.plainLanguage: Real-time text needs to be fast (a letter in 300 milliseconds), work with any language, connect to old phone text services, and let deaf people see who is typing.

sections.title: How ToIP Works
sections.content:
The implementation uses SIP to negotiate and control sessions, including media types, participant preferences, and language. RTP carries the actual text, using payload types text/t140 (for the raw text) and text/red (redundancy to recover lost characters). SDP (Session Description Protocol) describes the session in SIP messages to indicate text availability and capability.

Sessions can be point-to-point or multipoint (conferences). Users register preferences with the SIP registrar, and the server can enforce policy (for example, requiring a relay service). The system supports simultaneous text and voice, allowing users to hear and read at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP is the waiter that sets up the call and says text available. RTP is the truck that carries the letters. Both are standard internet protocols already used for voice and video.

sections.title: Connecting to Legacy Systems
sections.content:
A text gateway converts between ToIP and legacy text systems. The PSTN uses analog text phones (TTY or TDD, sending tones for characters), and the RFC requires gateways to handle Voice Carry Over (VCO, where users hear and send text) and Hearing Carry Over (HCO, where users send voice and hear text).

Mobile networks use different encodings: the Cellular Text Telephone Modem (CTM), Baudot modes, or data channels. Instant messaging is different (buffered, not streamed), so interworking is optional. Gateways must preserve caller ID and buffer to cope with timing differences.
sections.plainLanguage: Old text phones on phone lines use a different language. A gateway translator sits between the internet text call and the phone line, converting back and forth.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
Emergency services access must work: when a deaf caller uses ToIP to reach 911, the system should route to a relay service. Home gateways (adapters for phone lines) may need to bridge ToIP and PSTN text phones. User mobility requires that a person can call from any device; proxy servers and DNS are used for routing.

Quality of Service (QoS) and firewall traversal are important because text is time-sensitive; unlike email, a 5-second delay is unacceptable. The RFC recommends treating text like voice for QoS priority and planning for NAT traversal.
sections.plainLanguage: An emergency call, a call from a phone line device, or a call from abroad all need to work. The system must not drop letters even if the network is busy.
